Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, because mood changes are incredibly common and very treatable. Everything you share stays confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
Oh, yeah, I’ve still been laughing—maybe not as much as before the baby, but when my husband makes goofy faces at her or when she gets that milk-drunk look, I can’t help but chuckle.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—like when my little one does those tiny baby sneezes or when the dog tries to “help” during tummy-time. It’s not quite as spontaneous as before, but the funny moments are still there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Most days I do find myself looking forward to little things—like our morning walk to the mailbox or my favorite podcast during her nap. They’re small, but they still feel nice to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. I mean, if she’s fussy and I can’t figure out why, I might think “maybe I missed something,” but it’s just a quick thought—I don’t stay stuck on it or beat myself up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll catch myself worrying that her breathing sounds different or that she’s not eating enough, even when everything looks fine. It doesn’t last long and I can usually settle once I check on her, but yeah, it pops up.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that kind of sudden fear or panic—nothing like that.
Things have been getting on top of me

Now and then, when she’s had a couple of rough nights in a row or the laundry piles up, I’ll think “ugh, how am I going to get through all this?” But it’s more like a passing wave than feeling totally swamped.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s actually been okay. Once she settles for the night I can usually fall back asleep pretty easily—I’m tired, but not because I’m feeling unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t really felt sad or miserable. Tired, sure, but not down or weepy—overall I still feel pretty steady.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t had any of those “can’t-stop-crying” moments. I might get a little teary when a song comes on that reminds me of her growing so fast, but it’s brief and not from feeling unhappy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that has crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**

**Positive findings**  
- Intermittent, mild worry about infant’s health (breathing, feeding) without objective cause; resolves quickly after reassurance  
- Occasional sense of “getting on top of me” during clustered infant-care demands; described as “passing wave,” not persistent overwhelm  

**Absences / Negative findings**  
- No low mood, tearfulness, or anhedonia; enjoyment of baby and daily activities preserved  
- No inappropriate guilt or self-blame  
- No sleep disruption secondary to mood (sleep loss solely situational to infant needs)  
- No panic episodes, hopelessness, or self-harm ideation  

**Clinical impression**  
Responses indicate normal postpartum adjustment with mild situational anxiety. Patient retains capacity for pleasure, adaptive coping, and appropriate reality testing. No red-flag symptoms for major postpartum depression or anxiety disorder identified at this time. Continue routine postpartum follow-up and educate on signs warranting re-screening.
